additional_requirements: The binge eating occurs, on average, at least once a week for 3 months

S049.name: Eating_Large_Amount
S049.description: Eating, in a discrete period of time, an amount of food that is definitely larger than what most individuals would eat in a similar period of time under similar circumstances.
examples: Eating more than 3-4 times the amount of a typical meal within 2 hours.
Continuously eating large amounts of high-calorie snacks in addition to main meals.
Eating enough to empty a significant portion of the refrigerator or pantry at once.
Eating clearly more food than others during the same period of time.

S050.name: Loss_of_Control
S050.description: A sense of lack of control over eating during the episode (e.g., a feeling that one cannot stop eating or control what or how much one is eating).
examples: A feeling that once I start eating, I cannot stop even if I want to.
Thinking 'I shouldn't eat any more' but mechanically continuing to eat.
A feeling of helplessness that I cannot decide for myself how much to eat.
Eating as if my body is being controlled by someone else.

S051.name: Rapid_Eating
S051.description: Eating much more rapidly than normal.
examples: Swallowing food without chewing it properly.
Eating continuously and rapidly to the point where it is difficult to breathe.
Eating so urgently that there is no time to taste the food.
Eating at a speed that surprises others.

S052.name: Eating_Until_Uncomfortably_Full
examples: Eating until the stomach feels distended to the point of bursting and pain.
Eating so much that it is difficult to even stand up or move.
Continuing to eat until feeling nauseous or like vomiting.
Unable to stop eating even though it is physically uncomfortable and painful.

S054.name: Eating_Alone_Due_to_Embarrassment
S054.description: Eating alone because of feeling embarrassed by how much one is eating.
examples: Eating only when alone because of fear that others will think strangely of the amount eaten.
Eating secretly after family members have gone to sleep.
Pretending to eat little in front of people, then binging when alone.
Locking the door or eating in a secret place like a car to avoid being seen eating.

S055.name: Negative_Affect_After_Binge
S055.description: Feeling disgusted with oneself, depressed, or very guilty afterward.
examples: Feeling unbearable disgust and self-loathing after binging.
Falling into extreme depression and self-criticism immediately after binging.
Feeling intense guilt and regret over the fact that I binged again.
Feeling shame that I am pathetic and have weak willpower after binging.

symptom.disease_info: Binge-Eating Disorder is characterized by recurrent episodes of consuming unusually large amounts of food in a discrete period while experiencing a sense of loss of control over eating, without regular compensatory behaviors such as purging or excessive exercise. Episodes are typically associated with marked distress and patterns such as eating rapidly, eating when not physically hungry, eating alone due to embarrassment, or feeling disgusted or guilty afterward. The course is often chronic or relapsing, with severity influenced by frequency of episodes, associated psychological distress, and functional impact on work, relationships, and health. It is distinguished from bulimia nervosa primarily by the absence of regular compensatory behaviors and from normative overeating by the recurrent loss of control and significant associated distress.

patient.stressor: About six months ago, Roy was promoted from a familiar CNC role to an acting shift‑supervisor position on the night shift, which disrupted his long‑standing routines around meals, sleep, and church activities. The pressure of managing younger workers, covering mandatory overtime, and feeling responsible when production targets were missed left him coming home wired and hungry after midnight, often alone while his wife was already asleep. What began as grabbing extra takeout on the drive home evolved over about five months into frequent late‑night eating during game replays or woodworking sessions, becoming his main way to decompress from work stress. He finally agreed to see a psychiatrist after his pastor and wife both commented on his rapid weight gain, his avoidance of church potlucks out of embarrassment about how he was eating, and his own sense that his eating was "out of control" during those late hours.
patient.chief_complaint: “Once I start eating late at night after my shift, I feel like I can’t stop or control how much I’m eating.”

patient.stressor: Belinda’s youngest grandchild moved out of state with her daughter about seven months ago, leaving her house much quieter and her usual childcare responsibilities abruptly gone. With more unstructured evenings and fewer family dinners, she found herself baking and cooking the same rich Southern dishes she used to make for the grandkids, but now eating them largely on her own while watching Saints games or working on quilts. Over the following five months, she noticed that she was repeatedly eating much more than she intended during these solitary evenings, then staying up late doing PTA spreadsheets and feeling ashamed of how she had eaten. She sought psychiatric care after her primary doctor noted her rising blood pressure, suggested her eating patterns might be linked to emotional loneliness, and encouraged her to talk to someone when she admitted she was increasingly hiding how much she ate from friends at church socials.
patient.chief_complaint: “I’ve started eating big amounts by myself at night because I’m embarrassed for anyone to see how much I’m eating.”

patient.stressor: Dennis moved from his tight‑knit hometown to start college, but after struggling with his coursework and feeling out of place on campus, he decided to take a leave of absence and move back home about eight months ago. Losing his structured class schedule, intramural sports, and robotics club responsibilities left him spending long stretches alone in his room gaming and watching streams, while his friends remained busy with college life. Over the past five months, late‑night delivery runs and convenience‑store trips became his main comfort and break from boredom, and he found himself repeatedly finishing large amounts of food during gaming sessions in a way that felt very different from the occasional pizza with friends he was used to. He agreed to see a psychiatrist after his mother confronted him about the stack of fast‑food bags in his room and he realized that these eating episodes were happening more often, felt out of control, and were making him avoid social plans and pickup basketball because he was so self‑conscious about it.
patient.chief_complaint: “Lately when I’m home alone, I end up eating way more food at once than I think most people would, and it keeps happening.”
